blocks.x: Fall was always my favorite time to travel. It’s when the crowds have loosened their grip on Paris, the weather is better in Italy, and the hotel rates are lower in Marrakech. But over the last few years, I’ve noticed more and more travelers at airports near and far in September, October, and November. Indicating demand, plane tickets haven’t been dipping in the same way that they used to when the leaves turned. Open any news app, and you’ll see the headlines shouting from the rooftops: We are in the era of the “fallcation.”

“Savvy travelers are establishing autumn as the new peak season for global trips,” says John Clifford, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and founder of International Travel Management. He attributes this to the fact that more people are traveling than ever in the summertime, leading to crowded destinations. On top of that, summers are only getting hotter. All this, Clifford says, leads to people looking to take their big annual vacation outside of the summer season. The data backs it up: According to Virtuoso, the global network of luxury travel agencies and advisors, bookings for fall travel this year have increased by 59% compared to last year; the network’s agents report a 77% increase in September sales, making it a peak month for travel. October and November sales are up 54% and 71%, respectively.

Fall travel is increasing even to destinations in Asia, where the window between September and November is already the peak season. Catherine Heald, another CNT Top Travel Specialist and founder of Asia-focused Remote Lands, says her company has been seeing around 15% more fall bookings in the last few years. But nowhere is it more pronounced than in universally loved Italy, where September and October have become the height of the season, when it’s still “summer-like” in Southern Europe, says Gary Portuesi, a CNT Top Travel Specialist and a co-managing partner of Authentic Explorations. To Portuesi, fall in Italy now means November and December—and yes, they’re seeing a surge in bookings for those months too, when temperatures are cooler, crowds have dwindled, and hotel rates tend to drop. As he puts it, “It’s the new shoulder season.”

To learn more about the rise of the fallcation, I tapped a host of Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists to weigh in: Who’s actually traveling in the fall? Where are people going? And will we eventually have to avoid traveling in the fall, too? In a few years, will we be craving “summercations”? Here’s what the experts had to say.

At this point, it’s conventional wisdom that September, October, and November are more comfortable times to travel because, in most destinations, you get more temperate weather and fewer crowds in the fall. “Autumn has outperformed summer for at least the past two years,” says Tom Barber of UK-based Original Travel. For Barber, September and October departures are up by 53% and 45%, respectively, compared to August departures. He explains, “People still want the classic summer destinations—Greece, Italy, Spain, Egypt, Morocco—but they increasingly want to experience them without the intense heat.”

September is now one of the busiest months for travel company Red Savannah, says Camilla Davidson, its head of destination management for the UK, France, and Ireland. The relentless summer news cycle is also playing a part in this behavioral shift. “It’s all dominated by headlines around European wildfires, unlivable temperatures, endless lines on arrival at airports, overtourism, and elevated prices,” Davidson says. “Many savvy travelers are looking to shoulder seasons to avoid these pitfalls, with the fall seen as a more ‘reliable option’ than the spring.”

On the other hand, Cari Gray of Gray & Co., which focuses on private active trips, says that fall has always been her clients’ preferred travel period over the summer season. “So many folks have well-established summer routines like going to their cabins and annual visits to favorite lodges,” Gray says. “They break free in the fall when kids are in school—both in grade school and college—and the weather is perfect for outdoor activities.”
